1: Chapter 1: A Visitor on the Rainy Night
In Peñaseca it had been raining for three days. In spring, Lucía Romero’s older sister had left for Madrid, and since then Lucía had been running the village’s tiny pharmacy alone.
At nightfall she shut the shutters, counted the day’s takings, blew out the lamp, and went upstairs.
She had barely lain down when someone pounded hard on the downstairs door. A man’s voice asked: —Is anyone there?
On the threshold stood a youth soaked to the skin, his left arm wrapped in a blood‑stained cloth. He said his name was Diego Lobo and that he belonged to the Azure Dragon Society.
“I need you to treat me,” Lobo said in a low voice. “I can pay. Will three thousand five hundred reales be enough?”
He pulled a letter wrapped in waxed paper from his jacket. “This letter has to reach the monastery of San Blas before May eighteenth.”
For Lucía, stitching up that wound was a piece of cake, but the letter worried her.
Even so, she refused his money and simply said, “I’ll take him up to the mountain at dawn.”
2: At dawn they set off. Lucia carried on her back a basket with bread, medicinal herbs, and an old umbrella.

On the mountainside they ran into old Tomás Gil, who was splitting firewood. He laid down his axe and whispered that the night before three strangers had inquired at the village gate about a wounded youth.
“Take the trail, Lucía,” Tomás Gil said. “The main road isn’t safe.” Lucía thanked him.
The trail was narrow and slippery. Lucia walked ahead, stepping firmly with each step. Lobo followed silently behind.
At noon the rain stopped, the mist slowly cleared, and in the distance the roof of San Blas Monastery appeared. Waiting at the door was Sister Inés, the nun in charge of greeting visitors.
Sister Inés took the letter, examined the red seal, and nodded. “The abbess has been waiting two years for this letter.”
Lobo said to Lucía, “I owe you my life.” Lucía smiled. “Then the next time you come, fix the apothecary’s roof.” Lobo stayed at the monastery.
At dusk, Lucía descended the mountain alone. When she got home it was already night; she lit the lamp and sat a long while behind the counter.
